about: Short quotations of Anne Carson's own words, used as commentary on this folder's page (and its README). Educational demos made to show an open-source tool. Not research. Rule: a few only, one per work, each at most 15 words and a contiguous span (no ellipsis), never a whole poem or stanza; the exact wording was checked on the pages listed in 'sources', which reproduce it; attributed 'Anne Carson, <work> (<year>)'. The Committee-quoted line from Eros the Bittersweet is governed by CLAIMS.md L09 and is not in this list. Rows are listed in CLAIMS.md, section 'Quotations' (L61, a quotation from Autobiography of Red, was withdrawn: it did not comment on anything next to it). Only the quoted span itself is stored here: the surrounding words on each source page are not copied.

quotes.text: It was Sappho who first called eros 'bittersweet.'
quotes.context: The opening line of her first book, next to Sappho's word for Eros.

sources.kind: publisher page (Dalkey Archive); the page's blurb opens with the book's first sentence
essay (Emma Bolden, Tupelo Quarterly, 14 July 2020): the line is the essay's epigraph, credited to the book; independent of the blurb
reading notes (Sasha Martinez, Marginalia, 24 August 2011): the book's opening lines, copied from the book itself; independent of the blurb
distributor page (NewSouth Books): a copy of the publisher's blurb, not an independent witness

quotes.text: brackets imply a free space of imaginal adventure
quotes.work: If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho
quotes.context: From the introduction to her translation of Sappho's fragments, on the brackets that mark what a torn papyrus has lost.

sources.kind: review (Emily Wilson, London Review of Books, 8 January 2004)

quotes.placement_note: Her comment is about the brackets that stand for the holes in a torn papyrus, not about the editors' restorations inside brackets; keep it beside the lost-papyrus explanation.
